analysis.one_liner: Moves money creation from private banks to the Treasury and funds public programs with it.
analysis.headline: The bill to transfer money creation from private banks to the Treasury was referred to committee, received one subcommittee hearing, and died when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013 without ever reaching a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make money creation a government function only. Banks could no longer create money by lending against deposits — a practice known as fractional reserve banking — and anyone who did could face up to five years in prison. The Federal Reserve would be folded into the Treasury Department, and a new Monetary Authority inside Treasury would control how much money enters circulation. New government-created money would fund infrastructure grants to states, interest-free loans to cities and school boards, a path to paying off the national debt, an 8% cap on interest rates for consumer loans, and recommendations for universal college and health care funding.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary households would benefit from capped interest rates (8% APR on consumer loans, with total interest never exceeding the loan amount), an eventualCitizens Dividend recommendation, and government money spent directly into the economy for infrastructure, education, and health care rather than borrowed at interest from banks. State and local governments would get monetary grants and interest-free lending for schools, roads, and fire services. The federal government would stop paying interest on its own debt and currency.

how_it_helps.text: Caps annual interest rates at 8% inclusive of all fees, and limits total interest charges on any consumer loan (other than a mortgage) to the amount of the loan itself.
Requires the government to disperse annual grants to states equal to 25% of the money created in the prior year, for infrastructure, education, health care, pensions, and unfunded federal mandates.

Ends the government's reliance on borrowing: the Treasury would create money to cover shortfalls and pay off outstanding federal debt as it comes due, eliminating interest payments to bondholders over time.
Directs the Secretary to recommend interest-free federal lending to state and local governments, including school boards and fire services, for infrastructure improvements.

Establishes a program of recommendations for universal pre-kindergarten, fully funded elementary and secondary education, and universal college at public institutions, plus coverage of Social Security shortfalls and a path to universal health care funding.

analysis.who_pays: Commercial banks and the Federal Reserve System. Banks would lose the ability to create money through lending — their deposits would become held-in-trust customer property they could not lend against, with criminal penalties (up to 5 years imprisonment) for doing so. The Federal Reserve's Board of Governors would be dissolved and its functions moved under Treasury control. Banks could continue lending only money they actually own or borrow from the government.
analysis.who_pays_short: Commercial banks and the Federal Reserve

drawbacks.text: The bill eliminates interest on transaction accounts entirely, so depositors would no longer earn interest on checking and standard savings balances.

Giving a small appointed board inside the Treasury direct control over the entire money supply creates a real inflation risk; the bill relies on the Monetary Authority to keep money creation non-inflationary but provides no independent mechanism beyond reporting discrepancies above 0.5% to Congress each quarter.

The transition would be sweeping and fast: all federal debt, all bank deposits, all Federal Reserve notes, and the entire structure of banking would be converted within roughly one to two years, a level of simultaneous monetary change economists broadly consider highly disruptive even when sympathetic to the goals.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential upside is enormous — interest-free public spending capacity, capped consumer interest, paid-off national debt, and funded infrastructure and education at a moment of mass unemployment. But the bill is a radical one-stroke redesign of the entire monetary system, and the risks of inflation and transition failure are genuine and not fully addressed. Honest supporters would acknowledge that even sympathetic monetary reformers debated whether this design could work as written. What is not in doubt is that it never received serious legislative scrutiny: no markup, no vote, one subcommittee hearing.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Financial Services Committee, then to two of its subcommittees, got a single subcommittee hearing in May 2012, and died when the Congress ended in January 2013 without ever being scheduled for a committee markup or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Dennis Kucinich introduced the bill on September 21, 2011, joined by John Conyers as the bill's sole cosponsor.

It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Financial Services, and on October 21, 2011, split between the Subcommittee on Domestic Monetary Policy and Technology and the Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit.
The only recorded activity after referral was a subcommittee hearing held on May 8, 2012; no full committee markup, no committee vote, and no floor action ever followed.
The 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013, and all not-yenacted bills expire when a Congress ends, so the bill died at the subcommittee stage.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private banks kept the legal ability to create money through lending, and the Federal Reserve remained an independent institution outside the Treasury — the two features the bill was written to end. Anyone with a credit card, personal loan, or student loan kept paying whatever rates the market allowed rather than a capped 8%.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private banks and the Federal Reserve

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no roll call exists; both the sponsor and the sole cosponsor were Democrats, and the committee that declined to advance the bill was chaired by a Republican.

industries.note: The bill would end fractional reserve banking outright — deposits would become customer property held in trust that banks could not lend against, and creating money by lending would carry criminal penalties of up to five years. Banks' business model of creating credit against deposits, which the bill's own findings link to wealth concentration and the 2008 crisis, would be replaced by lending money they actually own or borrow from the Treasury.

The Fed would be dissolved as an independent body and absorbed into the Treasury, with its board gone and a Monetary Authority of nine Senate-confirmed members setting money supply policy. It would keep performing most functions, but under executive-branch oversight and full GAO auditing.

Outstanding Treasury debt would be paid off in full with new United States Money as instruments come due, eliminating future interest income for investors who hold federal debt while freeing the government from interest payments.

They would receive annual monetary grants equal to 25% of newly created money and access to interest-free federal lending for infrastructure, schools, and fire services — resources they currently must raise through bonds and taxes.
